name: The Exchange Sacrifice
summary: White gives a rook for the knight on f6 to open the bishop's diagonal, and the black king is mated in three.
intro: Winning a rook for a bishop or knight is called winning the exchange, worth roughly two pawns. Handing that back on purpose is an exchange sacrifice: you accept a small, permanent material loss to buy something the scoreboard cannot measure. It is a hallmark of mature positional play, and it is one of the hardest offers for a beginner to make.
boardCaption: White to move; the knight on f6 is the only thing standing between the b2-bishop and the black king.

sections.heading: The Idea
paragraphs: A rook is worth about five points and a minor piece about three, so an exchange sacrifice starts you two points down and expects the position to pay you back. The compensation is usually one of a short list: a knight parked on an outpost the rook could never occupy, a bishop raking a long diagonal that a defender used to block, a wrecked enemy pawn structure, a passed pawn nobody can stop, or the removal of the single piece holding an attack together.

The values are only bookkeeping. A rook needs open files and does nothing on a closed board; a knight sitting on a hole in the enemy camp can be worth more than either rook. So the honest question is never how many points you gave up, but what the piece you took was actually doing. If it was the one defender of the squares you want, its three points were the most valuable three points on the board.

sections.heading: The Line
paragraphs: Here the compensation is not subtle, it is forced mate. The bishop on b2 points down the a1-h8 diagonal at the black king's shelter, and the knight on f6 is the only thing in its way. So White plays 1.Rxf6, a rook for a knight, and Black recaptures 1...gxf6, since declining just leaves him a piece down. The pawn now sits on f6 and blocks the diagonal in the knight's place, which is exactly the point: unlike the knight, a pawn cannot move out of the way, and a pawn can be captured by the queen.

White finishes with 2.Rg1, check down the freshly opened g-file. The king cannot go to f8, occupied by his own rook, nor to f7 or h7, occupied by his own pawns, so 2...Kh8 is forced. Then 3.Qxf6 is mate: the queen takes the blocking pawn and gives check along the diagonal, defended by the bishop on b2 that started the whole idea. The king cannot escape to g8 or g7, both covered by the rook on g1, and the rook on f8 cannot capture on f6 because his own pawn on f7 is in the way. The black queen, buried on a8 behind a7 and b7, watches from four moves away.

sections.heading: How To Spot It
paragraphs: Look for an enemy minor piece that is doing a job no other piece can do, and count what happens when it disappears. Knights defending the squares in front of a castled king are the standard candidates, as are knights blockading a passed pawn or plugging a diagonal. If your rook is the only piece that can reach it, the exchange is a fair price. Note that White must take with the rook and not the bishop, since the bishop is the piece that guards the mating square.

Most exchange sacrifices are not mating attacks, though, and those are the harder ones to trust. There you are buying a long-term asset, and you must be honest about it: the asset has to be permanent. A shattered pawn structure cannot be repaired and an outpost defended by a pawn cannot be evicted, so those are worth paying for. A vague initiative is not. When you cannot calculate to a concrete finish, ask whether your compensation will still exist in twenty moves.

keyIdeas: The exchange is rook for minor piece, worth roughly two pawns.
You sacrifice it to buy something structural: a diagonal, an outpost, a broken structure.
Here 1.Rxf6 removes the only piece blocking the bishop on b2.
After 1...gxf6 the pawn blocks the diagonal, but the queen can capture it.
2.Rg1+ Kh8 3.Qxf6 is mate, the b2-bishop guarding the queen.
Take with the rook, not the bishop: the bishop supports the mate.
